title: Enterprise solution storyline and negotiation cheatsheet
author: Maya Hernandez
body:
Executive summary
-----------------
This document provides a compact, sales-ready storyline for enterprise prospects evaluating Redwood Inference, plus a negotiation cheatsheet that aligns pricing levers, technical tradeoffs, and security assurances. It bundles positioning statements for C-suite and engineering audiences, a short competitive snapshot, a pricing example matrix for common deal shapes, two lighthouse case studies with measurable outcomes, and a security FAQ designed for pre-RFP discussions. Use this as the canonical reference for field motions where Dedicated or Private deployment is under consideration.

Primary objectives
- Enable account teams to articulate Redwood's differentiation in performance, cost, and operational control.
- Provide concrete negotiation levers and suggested concession guardrails.
- Offer technical talking points and an on-the-spot security FAQ so sellers can respond quickly to common RFP/security questions.

Audience and use cases
- Executive sponsor (CIO/CTO): focus on strategic value — reliability, cost predictability, vendor risk reduction.
- Platform/ML lead: emphasize performance, model-management, rollout controls, and observability.
- Procurement and legal: emphasize SLAs, data residency, and contract levers.
- Solution architect/SE: use the technical appendix and benchmark snippets during demos and pilots.

Core positioning pillars (elevator + expansion)
1) Predictable production economics
   - Elevator: "Same inference API across hosted, dedicated, and private so you control cost without rebuilding."
   - Expand: Reserved Dedicated capacity, autoscaling burst policies, and per-route token breakdowns in Redwood Console give teams predictable spend and visible unit economics to tune batching and caching.
2) Production-grade reliability and graceful degradation
   - Elevator: "SLO-first runtime with automatic fallbacks keeps customer experiences online under load."
   - Expand: Multi-variant routing, region failover, and automatic model fallback policies with configurable priorities.
3) Developer-first operational experience
   - Elevator: "Ship faster: familiar REST/SDKs, streaming, function/tool calling, and first-class evals to prevent regressions."
   - Expand: Model versioning, canary rollouts, and token-level tracing that map to cost and latency.
4) Security and compliance for regulated workloads
   - Elevator: "Private deployments with customer-managed VPCs, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs."
   - Expand: On-prem packaging, SOC/ISO artifacts (see related compliance pages), and fine-grained RBAC.

Competitive snapshot (one-page)
Columns: Competitor | Strength | Weakness vs Redwood | Typical win criteria
- Competitor A (Managed model endpoints) | Easy managed hosting | Less focus on cost controls and rollout tooling | Price-sensitive, low-SLA internal apps
- Competitor B (Open-source runtime vendors) | Deep execution optimizations | Heavy operational lift and no unified hosted product | Teams with ops capacity to self-host
- Competitor C (Large cloud LLM API) | Broad model catalog and scale | Opaque performance-to-cost metrics and fewer private deployment controls | Organizations choosing convenience over control

Key battlecard points (quick rebuttals)
- "Your pricing is higher than public API." -> "We often lower total TCO because of reserved capacity, batching/caching, and quantization guidance; we can run a 30-day cost forecast from your token distribution."
- "We will self-host to avoid vendor lock-in." -> "Redwood supports private deployments and a consistent API and rollout surface so you can avoid rebuilding orchestration and observability."
- "Latency matters more than cost." -> "We prioritize latency SLOs with routing and optimized kernel selection; Dedicated SKUs are calibrated for low tail latency."

Pricing guidance and negotiation levers
- Typical deal shapes
  1) Pilot (Proof-of-Value): 1–3 months, hosted or small Dedicated pool, fixed credit for usage + professional services (PS) to instrument evals.
  2) Mid-market subscription: Reserved Dedicated nodes with monthly commit, burst capacity, 6–12 month term.
  3) Enterprise Private: On-prem or VPC private deployment, annual license + support + optional managed services.

- Componentized pricing levers (use these in negotiation)
  - Base subscription / reserved capacity: commitment term and unit count (nodes / throughput).
  - Burst credits: limited pay-as-you-go for spikes.
  - Managed services / SRE runbook: optional for Private deployments, usually priced as FTE-equivalent monthly fee.
  - Observability retention: longer retention windows are an add-on.
  - Professional services: onboarding, custom quantization, and eval creation.

- Example pricing matrix (illustrative numbers for field use only)
  - Pilot: $25k–$75k total (1–3 month), includes 1 TB of tokens-equivalent credits and 40 hours PS.
  - Mid-market Dedicated: $12k/month reserved (baseline) for steady throughput with 25% burst over commit; 12-month term; volume discounts at 3–6 month consumption triggers.
  - Enterprise Private: $250k–$800k/year license depending on scale, plus 10–20% annual support fee and optional managed SRE at $40k–$120k/year.

Negotiation cheatsheet (concession guardrails)
- Always ask for a baseline commitment in exchange for material discounts (commits reduce unit economics for Redwood).
- Offer limited-time onboarding credits for pilots (one-off), not ongoing discounts.
- For security-sensitive customers, package compliance deliverables as scoped professional services rather than discounted product line items.
- Keep observability retention and managed SRE as upsell items; concede only up to one quarter of retention at the initial term.

Pitch deck outline (10-slide, field-ready)
1) Cover: Customer logo, Redwood logo, one-line value prop.
2) Why now: market trends and cost/latency pain.
3) Solution summary: Redwood product modes and how they map to customer requirements.
4) Differentiators: production-first runtime, cost controls, unified API.
5) Architecture diagram: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (annotate security controls).
6) SLA and reliability guarantees.
7) Pricing and proposed deal shape (from matrix).
8) Pilot plan and success criteria.
9) Lighthouse case study summary.
10) Next steps and ask (technical deep dive, security questionnaire, PO).

Lighthouse case studies (short)
1) FinOps SaaS: customer reduced per-response cost by 38% after migrating to Dedicated with prefix caching and quantization recommendations. Key outcomes: 20% latency improvement (p50), 38% cost reduction, and predictable monthly spend enabling finance-backed commitments.
2) Regulated healthcare platform: deployed Redwood Private in VPC with HSM KMS integration; enabled PHI-compliant inference and cut deployment time from 12 weeks (in-house build) to 5 weeks (Redwood delivery + PS). Key outcomes: SOC artifacts provided, audit log ingestion into customer's SIEM, and SLA for latency and uptime.

Security FAQ (pre-RFP, top questions and suggested field responses)
Q: How do you isolate customer data in Dedicated and Private?
A: Dedicated uses tenant-isolated GPU pools with strict network segmentation. Private deployments are customer-managed; data never leaves the VPC unless explicitly configured. We provide audit logs and optional HSM/KMS integrations.

Q: Do you retain model inputs or outputs?
A: By default, hosted logs are retained for operational and security debugging for X days (configurable). For Dedicated and Private, retention policies can be configured or disabled per contract. For regulated customers, we support zero-retention modes and can provide contractual commitments.

Q: What compliance artifacts do you provide?
A: We maintain SOC2 Type II documentation and can provide ISO27001 summary packages. For Private customers, we provide deployment checklists and assist in scoping penetration testing. See related compliance pages for the full artifact list.

Q: How do you handle vulnerability disclosures and patching for Private deployments?
A: We operate a coordinated disclosure policy. For Private on-prem packages, Redwood provides patch bundles and recommended maintenance windows; options for managed patching via a support add-on are available.

Operational readiness checklist for pilots (what SEs must validate)
1) Success criteria defined (latency, throughput, accuracy, cost).
2) Token distribution and sample prompts provided to Redwood for pre-flight tuning.
3) Network connectivity validated (VPN / VPC peering / firewall rules).
4) Security questionnaire handed to security team; identify required artifacts.
5) Observability hooks defined (traces, logs, cost dashboard access).

Objection handling scripts (short templates)
- "We need more proof of reliability." -> "We map your SLOs to a Dedicated baseline and present AWD-based traces from similar customers; we can include a canary rollout and SLA-backed penalty language in the pilot agreement."
- "We cannot commit budget yet." -> "Offer a short, scoped pilot with limited credits and a clear success definition tied to a PO or LOI — eliminates procurement friction and surfaces measurable ROI."
